people: Artemio V. Panganiban (author; ponente of Veterans and Ang Bagong Bayani)
Then-incoming President (BBM, unnamed in Duterte's appeal)

stances.claim: The party-list system was borrowed from European parliaments and grafted onto the Philippines's US-style presidential system, producing 'a mongrel without any historical, political, or social anchor in our country.' It was conceived as an 'experiment' to give the marginalized and underrepresented a better chance to become lawmakers.

Author's own two early ponencias resolved the textual ambiguities: Veterans v. Comelec (October 6, 2000) upheld the 2% threshold and ruled the 20% constitutional allocation 'directory, not mandatory'; Ang Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (June 26, 2001) limited eligibility to parties and nominees 'who belong to the marginalized and underrepresented sectors' -- quoting the Court that 'The law crafted to address the peculiar disadvantages of the Payatas hovel dwellers cannot be appropriated by the mansion owners of Forbes Park.' Reiterated unanimously in Partido ng Manggagawa v. Comelec (March 15, 2006) and Cibac v. Comelec (April 13, 2007); later extended to exclude major parties.

These early decisions also asked Congress to enact clarifying legislation. 'Sadly, Congress did not heed the Court.' Meanwhile, advocates of verba legis and dura lex sed lex criticized the Court (and CJ in particular) for 'allegedly sacrificing the letter of the law in favor of the intent of the framers.'

After CJ's retirement, the Court reversed course: Banat v. Comelec (April 21, 2009) voided the 2% bar; Atong Paglaum v. Comelec (April 2, 2013) ruled that party-list candidates and nominees need not belong to the marginalized and underrepresented -- 'thereby opening the party-list to everyone.'

The consequences of the reversals are visible: 'the dynasts, the tradpols, the rich, and the powerful invaded the system, misused it to circumvent the three-term constitutional limit, and misrepresented the lowly and the weak.' Further, the House now funds 63 party-list solons (constituting 20% of total) and 'grant[s] them pork-barrel-like insertions and reinventions.'

Three general solutions are available. First, amend the party-list law -- but as the May 17 Inquirer editorial put it, 'party-list representatives [and their allies, if I may add] who have gamed the system can hardly be expected to initiate any change.' Second, amend the Constitution via a constitutional convention (NOT a constituent assembly of incumbent Congress) -- but the Inquirer editorial called this 'a cure worse than the disease' because it would let 'the wicked' overhaul the better parts of the Charter. Third -- and most efficient -- the Supreme Court can overturn Banat and Atong Paglaum 'by simply reinstating its first two decisions, via a proper petition filed by the proper parties.'

notable_anecdotes: The Ang Bagong Bayani quotation preserved verbatim -- 'The intent of the Constitution is clear: to give genuine power to the people, not only by giving more law to those who have less in life, but more so by enabling them to become veritable lawmakers themselves... The law crafted to address the peculiar disadvantages of the Payatas hovel dwellers cannot be appropriated by the mansion owners of Forbes Park.' -- modeling the most-quoted Panganiban-era passage on the party-list system.

Author's self-disclosure: 'These two early decisions (Veterans and Ang Bagong Bayani) that I had the honor of writing for the Court...' -- flagging authorial connection to the doctrine he now defends.

The post-retirement reversal narrative: 'After I had retired, the Court... heeded the critics and voided the two-percent bar... and... ruled that the party-list candidates and their nominees need not belong to the marginalized and underrepresented, thereby opening the party-list to everyone.' -- a personally-stinging-but-restrained reflection on doctrinal repudiation.
The 'dynasts, tradpols, rich, and powerful' diagnosis paired with 'pork-barrel-like insertions and reinventions' -- preserved as the column's pointed structural-corruption descriptor.

Three-solution closing with author-preferred SC-overturn pathway: 'After all, if it could reverse its two earliest decisions, it could likewise easily solve this befuddling fiasco by simply reinstating its first two decisions, via a proper petition filed by the proper parties.' -- a quiet invitation to litigators.

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to President Duterte's 'Talk to the People' appeal for his successor 'to abolish the party-list system,' Panganiban diagnoses the party-list system as 'a mongrel without any historical, political, or social anchor in our country' -- borrowed from European parliaments and grafted onto a US-style presidential framework, conceived as an 'experiment' to give 'the marginalized and underrepresented a better chance to be lawmakers.' The Constitution allocates 20% of total representatives to party-list reps and dedicates half of those seats (for three consecutive terms after ratification) to the marginalized, but left the rest to Congress, which passed RA 7941 (the Party-list System Act) imposing a 2% threshold. CJ then traces his own two ponencias: Veterans v. Comelec (October 6, 2000) upheld the 2% threshold and ruled the 20% allocation 'directory, not mandatory'; Ang Bagong Bayani v. Comelec (June 26, 2001) limited eligibility to parties and nominees 'who belong to the marginalized and underrepresented sectors,' with the Court holding that 'The law crafted to address the peculiar disadvantages of the Payatas hovel dwellers cannot be appropriated by the mansion owners of Forbes Park.' These were unanimously reiterated in Partido ng Manggagawa v. Comelec (March 15, 2006) and Cibac v. Comelec (April 13, 2007), and extended to exclude major parties already represented in district polls. The decisions also called on Congress to enact clarifying legislation -- but 'Sadly, Congress did not heed the Court.' Meanwhile, advocates of 'verba legis' and 'dura lex sed lex' accused the Court (and CJ in particular) of 'sacrificing the letter of the law in favor of the intent of the framers.' After CJ's retirement, the Court reversed course: Banat v. Comelec (April 21, 2009) voided the 2% bar, and Atong Paglaum v. Comelec (April 2, 2013) ruled that party-list candidates and nominees need not belong to the marginalized and underrepresented -- 'thereby opening the party-list to everyone.' Consequences: 'the dynasts, the tradpols, the rich, and the powerful invaded the system, misused it to circumvent the three-term constitutional limit, and misrepresented the lowly and the weak'; the House now funds 63 party-list solons (20% of total) with 'pork-barrel-like insertions and reinventions.' CJ proposes three solutions: (1) amend the party-list law -- but the May 17 Inquirer editorial observed that 'party-list representatives [and their allies] who have gamed the system can hardly be expected to initiate any change'; (2) amend the Constitution via a constitutional convention (not a constituent assembly of incumbent Congress) -- but the Inquirer called this 'a cure worse than the disease' because it would let 'the wicked' overhaul better parts of the Charter; (3) have the Supreme Court overturn Banat and Atong Paglaum 'by simply reinstating its first two decisions, via a proper petition filed by the proper parties' -- the path CJ implicitly prefers.
